newsitem.title: USA: U.S. steps up pro-Turkey campaign.
newsitem.headline: U.S. steps up pro-Turkey campaign.

text.p: The United States, increasingly concerned about anti-Turkey sentiment, has stepped up its campaign to persuade European allies to keep Western institutions open to Ankara for membership, the State Department said Tuesday.
Spokesman Nicholas Burns hailed Turkey's recent adoption of a human rights reform package and said Europe should give Ankara "high marks" for this effort.

He disclosed that Carey Cavanaugh, whom he called the State Department's "point person" on Cyprus, is in Europe this week discussing efforts to resolve the Cyprus problem and other Greek-Turkey tensions. Cavanaugh has been in London and will also visit Brussels, Germany, the Hague and Paris.
American ambassadors in European capitals have been directed to reaffirm to their host governments the United States' "very strong views" on this matter, Burns said.
"We strongly believe the European Union should allow for the possibility of Turkish membership in the future," he said.
"Turkey is a European country. Turkey has its roots in Europe. Turkey's security is based in Europe. And Turkey's future, we believe, ought to be grounded in Europe," he added.
Washington acted after leading centrist EU politicians meeting in Brussels last week gave Turkey its bluntest warning to date that it would be locked out of the European Union.

Burns said "a number of our embassies, our ambassadors and other senior officials have spoken to European governments quite recently under instructions from Washington to reaffirm the very strong views of the United States" on Turkey.
He acknowleded that the United States does not have a vote in the European Union and "that we don't always see eye-to-eye with the European governments" on the matter of Turkey.

"But we very respectfully submit to our European friends that they must strategically think of Turkey as a European country and not send negative signals to Turkey -- some of the kind of signals that we've seen emanating from European governments over the last couple of weeks," he said.
The customs union between the European Union and Turkey -- which was supposed to be a step leading to full EU membership for Ankara -- "is a good, positive thing for both," he said.
In their comment on Turkey in Brussels, centrist European politicians reaffirmed that Turkey must improve its human rights record before it could be considered for EU membership.
Burns noted Turkey's parliament last week passed a new human rights reform package, including reduction in pretrial detention periods and early access to an attorney for accused.

He called this "an important step forward in improving Turkey's human rights performance" and urged rapid implementation to bring "Turkey's human rights picture more into line with its clear international obligations."
"We hope the European governments will take note of the fact that the Turkish government promoted this human rights package," he said, adding:

"That's an important consideration. The European governments often raise human rights concerns. Turkey now is trying to do something about it, and we think we should give the Turks high marks for this effort. Now we need to see the implementation."
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright stressed the U.S. view on Turkey on her recent six-country European tour.
